lead: Drying is not one speed. A wet solid first loses surface water at a steady rate, then slows as water must travel from inside. The drying rate curve plots rate R against moisture X and makes both stages visible. Its shape is measured in a simple batch test: weigh the sample, convert to X, differentiate, divide by drying area. The drying time is (m<sub>s</sub>/A) times the area under the 1/R curve between the two moistures, with m<sub>s</sub> in kg dry solid and A in m². This is how batch times, dryer capacity and the effect of air conditions are estimated before sizing equipment.
prereq: You need Chapter 7.6 for moisture content X, equilibrium moisture X* and bound and free water.

sections.h3: From weighings to a rate curve

blocks.text: A batch drying test uses a thin sample in air at fixed dry-bulb temperature, humidity and velocity. Record the sample mass m at times t. If m<sub>s</sub> is the dry-solid mass, then X = (m − m<sub>s</sub>)/m<sub>s</sub> kg water per kg dry solid. Plot X against t; the slope dX/dt at each point is negative. The drying rate is R = −(m<sub>s</sub>/A)(dX/dt), where A is the exposed drying area in m² and R is kg water evaporated per m² per hour. The dry-solid mass m<sub>s</sub> carries units kg dry solid.

items: Dry a known wet sample at constant air conditions.
Weigh it at fixed intervals and compute X at each time.
Draw X against t and find slopes dX/dt.
Multiply by −m<sub>s</sub>/A to get R at each X.
Plot R against X; mark the flat part and the fall.

blocks.where: R is drying rate in kg/(m²·h); m<sub>s</sub> is dry-solid mass in kg; A is drying area in m²; X is moisture in kg/kg dry solid; t is time in h.

sections.h3: Constant rate, critical point, falling rate

blocks.text: In the constant-rate period the surface is wet. Water evaporates as from a free liquid surface, so R stays at R<sub>c</sub>. This ends at the critical moisture X<sub>c</sub>, when the surface can no longer supply free water. Below X<sub>c</sub> the rate falls. In a simple linear falling-rate stage the rate falls in proportion to the free moisture above X*: R = R<sub>c</sub>(X − X*)/(X<sub>c</sub> − X*). Here X* is the equilibrium moisture, the value at which drying stops. Many solids show a second, slower diffusion-controlled stage near dryness.
The constant rate can be predicted from the air. The surface sits at the wet-bulb temperature, and the heat convected to it is all used to evaporate water:

blocks.where: R<sub>c</sub> is the constant drying rate in kg/(m²·s); h is the heat-transfer coefficient in W/(m²·K); T and T<sub>w</sub> are the dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures of the air; λ<sub>w</sub> is the latent heat at T<sub>w</sub> in J/kg; G is the air mass velocity in kg/(m²·h). The correlation for h is for air flowing parallel to the surface, G from about 2450 to 29 300 kg/(m²·h).
t<sub>c</sub> is constant-rate time in h; X₁ is initial moisture; X<sub>c</sub> is critical moisture; R<sub>c</sub> is constant drying rate; other symbols as before.

blocks.text: t<sub>f</sub> = (m<sub>s</sub> (X<sub>c</sub> − X*)/(A R<sub>c</sub>)) ln((X<sub>c</sub> − X*)/(X₂ − X*))
blocks.where: t<sub>f</sub> is falling-rate time in h; X<sub>c</sub> − X* is free moisture at the critical point; R<sub>c</sub> is the constant drying rate in kg/(m²·h); A is drying area in m²; m<sub>s</sub> is dry-solid mass in kg; X₂ is final moisture above X*; ln is the natural logarithm. Use this for one straight falling line ending at X*.

blocks.text: If X₂ is above X<sub>c</sub>, only t<sub>c</sub> applies. If X₂ is below X<sub>c</sub>, total time is t<sub>c</sub> + t<sub>f</sub>. For a curved falling stage, integrate graphically: t = (m<sub>s</sub>/A) ∫ dX/R from X₂ to X₁, which is the area under the 1/R curve.

Higher air temperature and lower humidity raise R<sub>c</sub> and often X<sub>c</sub>, because evaporation is faster. Air velocity raises R<sub>c</sub> by thinning the boundary layer, but it barely changes the falling-rate period, where internal diffusion controls. Doubling the bed thickness roughly doubles m<sub>s</sub>/A and the time, but a thick bed can dry unevenly. Shrinkage reduces A, so the real rate falls faster than the ideal line. Case hardening seals the surface, trapping water inside and adding a slow second falling stage. The measured curve, not a single formula, is the safe basis for design.

figure.caption: The rate curve of the first worked example. The rate is flat at R<sub>c</sub> = 1.5 kg/(m²·h) down to the critical moisture X<sub>c</sub> = 0.20, then falls in a straight line to zero at X* = 0.05. The shaded band is the drying asked for, from X = 0.40 to 0.10: 6.67 h at constant rate and 5.49 h on the falling line, 12.2 h in all.

spec.aria: Drying rate against moisture content: a flat line at 1.5 from 0.40 down to 0.20, then a straight line falling to zero at 0.05. The final moisture 0.10 is marked on the falling line, and the times 6.67 hours and 5.49 hours are written on the two parts.

examples.question: A batch dryer holds 50 kg of dry solid with an exposed drying area A = 1 m². The solid is dried from X₁ = 0.40 to X₂ = 0.10 kg/kg dry solid. Tests give X<sub>c</sub> = 0.20, X* = 0.05 and R<sub>c</sub> = 1.5 kg/(m²·h). Find the constant-rate time, falling-rate time and total drying time.
steps: Dry-solid mass m<sub>s</sub> = 50 kg; area A = 1 m²; R<sub>c</sub> = 1.5 kg/(m²·h).
Initial moisture X₁ = 0.40 is above X<sub>c</sub> = 0.20, so a constant-rate period exists.
Constant-rate time: t<sub>c</sub> = (m<sub>s</sub>/(A R<sub>c</sub>))(X₁ − X<sub>c</sub>) = (50/(1 × 1.5))(0.40 − 0.20) h = 33.33 × 0.20 h = 6.67 h.
Final moisture X₂ = 0.10 is below X<sub>c</sub>, so the falling-rate period follows.
For one straight falling line to X* = 0.05: t<sub>f</sub> = (m<sub>s</sub> (X<sub>c</sub> − X*)/(A R<sub>c</sub>)) ln((X<sub>c</sub> − X*)/(X₂ − X*)).
Total time t = t<sub>c</sub> + t<sub>f</sub> = 6.67 + 5.49 h = 12.16 h, about 12.2 h.
examples.answer: The constant-rate time is 6.67 h, the falling-rate time is 5.49 h and the total drying time is about 12.2 h.
examples.check:
import math
m<sub>s</sub> = 50.0
A = 1.0
R<sub>c</sub> = 1.5
X1 = 0.40
Xc = 0.20
X2 = 0.10
Xstar = 0.05
t<sub>c</sub> = (m<sub>s</sub>/(A*R<sub>c</sub>))*(X1-Xc)
t<sub>f</sub> = (m<sub>s</sub>*(Xc-Xstar)/(A*R<sub>c</sub>))*math.log((Xc-Xstar)/(X2-Xstar))
print(f"{t<sub>c</sub>:.2f}")
print(f"{t<sub>f</sub>:.2f}")
print(f"{t<sub>c</sub>+t<sub>f</sub>:.1f}")

examples.question: Air at 65 °C with Y = 0.010 kg/kg dry air flows at 3.5 m/s parallel to the surface of a tray of wet solid. Its wet-bulb temperature is 28.8 °C and its humid volume 0.973 m³/kg dry air. Predict the constant drying rate.
steps: Mass velocity: G = 1.038 × 3.5 × 3600 = 13 080 kg/(m²·h), inside the range of the correlation.
Latent heat at 28.8 °C: λ<sub>w</sub> ≈ 2433 kJ/kg = 2.433 × 10⁶ J/kg.
examples.answer: The constant drying rate is about 2.15 kg/(m²·h). Doubling the air speed would raise it by 2<sup>0.8</sup> = 1.74 times.

examples.question: A curved falling-rate stage was measured on a solid with m<sub>s</sub>/A = 25 kg/m². The rates R in kg/(m²·h) at X = 0.20, 0.16, 0.12, 0.08 and 0.06 are 1.50, 1.25, 0.95, 0.60 and 0.38. Find the time to dry from X = 0.20 to 0.06 by graphical integration.
steps: Total area under the 1/R curve = 0.1638 m²·h/kg.
Check: a straight falling line through the origin from R = 1.50 at X = 0.20 would give 25 × (0.20/1.50) ln(0.20/0.06) = 4.01 h, close because the data lie near that line.
examples.answer: The falling-rate time is about 4.1 h.

traps: Using the constant-rate formula below X<sub>c</sub>: t<sub>c</sub> = (m<sub>s</sub>/(A R<sub>c</sub>))(X₁ − X<sub>c</sub>) stops at X<sub>c</sub>, even when X₂ is lower.
Forgetting that R<sub>c</sub> is per m² of drying area, not per kg of solid; the factor m<sub>s</sub>/A must appear.
Putting X₂ = X* in the log formula divides by zero; the final moisture must be above X*.
Expecting air velocity to speed the falling-rate period; it mainly changes R<sub>c</sub>.
Mixing X on a dry basis with wet-basis moisture; these formulas use kg water per kg dry solid.

quiz.a: The moisture content at which the constant-rate period ends and the falling-rate period begins.

quiz.q: Why does the drying rate stay constant at first?
quiz.a: The surface remains wet, so water evaporates as from a free liquid surface and the rate is set by the air conditions.

quiz.q: A solid has m<sub>s</sub>/A = 20 kg/m², R<sub>c</sub> = 2.0 kg/(m²·h), X₁ = 0.35 and X<sub>c</sub> = 0.15. Find the constant-rate time.
Air velocity is doubled during the falling-rate period. What happens to the drying time and why?
quiz.a: The time changes little. The rate is controlled by diffusion of water inside the solid, not by the air boundary layer at the surface.

quiz.q: Why is X* subtracted in the falling-rate driving force?
quiz.a: X* is the equilibrium moisture. No net drying occurs at X*, so the driving force is the free moisture X − X*.

quiz.q: For X<sub>c</sub> = 0.20, X* = 0.04, X₂ = 0.09, m<sub>s</sub>/A = 30 kg/m² and R<sub>c</sub> = 1.2 kg/(m²·h), find the falling-rate time.
A real drying curve shows a sharp second fall near dryness. Give two reasons.
quiz.a: Shrinkage reduces the drying area, and case hardening seals the surface so water diffuses more slowly from inside.

beyond: Not for the exam. Drying curves are measured for each food, pharmaceutical and ceramic product, because shrinkage, cracking and colour set the safe air temperature. Search for drying kinetics, characteristic drying curve and case hardening.
